title.en: Ptah Creates by Heart and Tongue: The Memphite Theology
title.zh: 卜塔以心與舌創世：孟菲斯神學

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (temple of Ptah, city of the artificer god)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（工藝之神卜塔神廟）

texts.period: Memphite doctrine (Shabaka Stone copy, 25th Dynasty); retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (London, 1913), ch. VI, 'The City of the Elf God'

summary.en: Memphis' own account of creation: Ptah, chief of the eight dwarfish Khnumu, first appeared as an egg laid by the chaos goose and fashioned the sun egg and the moon egg on his potter's wheel; in the higher doctrine the Memphite priests eulogize him as 'the mind and tongue of the gods', the creator whose ideas take material shape the moment he gives them expression.
summary.zh: 孟菲斯之創世記：卜塔，八位矮小庫努姆之首，初為混沌鵝所生之卵，於陶輪上造太陽之卵與月亮之卵；其高階教義則謂他為『眾神之心與舌』——其意念一經表達，即化為實物。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Memphite theology retold in a public-domain synthesis (Mackenzie 1913); all passages are his retelling, marked as such. The Shabaka Stone's own text is fragmentary; Mackenzie's rendering preserves the heart-and-tongue doctrine.

passages.text: At the beginning, according to Memphite belief, Ptah shaped the world and the heavens, assisted by his eight workmen, the dwarfish Khnumu. He was also the creator of mankind, and in Egyptian tombs are found numerous earthenware models of these 'elves', who were believed to have had power to reconstruct the decaying bodies of the dead. As their dwellings were underground, they may have also been 'artisans of vegetation', like the spirits associated with Tvashtar, the 'master workman' of the Rig-Veda hymns and the 'black dwarfs' of Teutonic mythology.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. VI.

passages.text: Like Ra, Ptah was also believed to have first appeared as an egg, which, according to one of the many folk beliefs of Egypt, was laid by the chaos goose which came to be identified with Seb, the earth god, and afterwards with the combined deities Amon-Ra. Ptah, as the primeval 'artificer god', was credited with making 'the sun egg' and also 'the moon egg', and a bas-relief at Philae shows him actively engaged at the work, using his potter's wheel.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. VI.

passages.text: A higher and later conception of Ptah represents him as a sublime creator god who has power to call into existence each thing he names. He is the embodiment of mind from which all things emerge, and his ideas take material shape when he gives them expression. In a philosophic poem a Memphite priest eulogizes the great deity as 'the mind and tongue of the gods', and even as the creator of other gods as well as of 'all people, cattle, and reptiles', the sun, and the habitable world.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. VI.

title.en: The War of the Gods at Heracleopolis: The Great Cat and the Fiery Door
title.zh: 赫拉克利奧波利斯之諸神之戰：巨貓與火門

region.en: Heracleopolis Magna (Khenen-su), Middle Egypt (the lakes of natron and of truth)
region.zh: 埃及中埃及赫拉克利奧波利斯（ natron 湖與真理湖）

texts.period: Heracleopolitan theology of the 9th-10th Dynasties; retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XIV, 'Father Gods and Mother Goddesses'

summary.en: The local creation myth of Heracleopolis: Ra rises from the deep as the sun egg or the lotus flower — 'He who said: I am but One... He who is Yesterday (Osiris) and the Morrow (Ra)'; in its two sacred lakes Ra cleanses himself; at the height of the war of the gods Set flings filth in Horus' face and Horus mutilates Set, until Ra, as the Great Cat of the Persea tree, strangles the Apep serpent; and at the door of the fiery region crouches the greyhound-headed devourer of the condemned.
summary.zh: 赫拉克利奧波利斯本地創世記：拉以日卵或蓮花自深處升起——『彼自言：吾乃唯一……彼乃昨日（奧西里斯）與明日（拉）』；於其二聖湖中淨身；諸神之戰方酣，塞特擲穢於荷魯斯之面，荷魯斯殘塞特之體；末則拉化身為柏塞亞樹間之巨貓，勒斃阿波菲斯之蛇；火獄之門蹲踞著灰犬首之噬魂者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient theology retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling. The Great Cat of Heliopolis slashing the Apep serpent is the scene depicted in BD ch. 17 vignettes.

passages.text: Heracleopolis Magna, which the Egyptians called Khenen-su is of special mythological interest. It came to be recognized as the scene of the great creation myth of the sun worshippers. There Ra, at the beginning, rose from the primeval deep in the form of the sun egg, or the lotus flower — He that openeth and he that closeth the door; He who said: 'I am but One'. Ra, who was produced by himself; Whose various names make up the group of gods; He who is Yesterday (Osiris) and the Morrow (Ra).
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XIV.

passages.text: Khenen-su district was the scene of the 'war of the gods', who contended against one another at Ra's command — a myth which suggests the everlasting struggle between the forces of nature, which began at Creation's dawn, and is ever controlled by the sun. Somewhere in the nome were situated the two mythical lakes, 'the lake of natron' and 'the lake of truth', in which Ra cleansed himself, and there, too, at the height of their great struggle — symbolized as the struggle between good and evil — Set flung filth in the face of Horus, and Horus mutilated Set. The ultimate victory was due to Ra, who, in the form of the Great Cat that haunted the Persea tree at Heliopolis, fought with the Apep serpent and overcame it.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XIV.

passages.text: In the vicinity of Khenen-su was the fiery region. At its entrance crouched the demon who had human skin and the head of a greyhound. He was concealed by the door, and pounced unexpectedly upon 'the damned'; he tore out their hearts, which he devoured, and he swallowed their spirits. So the faithful sun worshippers were wont to pray: 'O Ra-tum give me deliverance from the demon who devoureth those who are condemned — he who waits at the door of the fiery place and is not seen. Save me from him who clutcheth souls, and eateth all filth and rottenness by day and by night. Those who dread him are helpless.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XIV.

passages.text: At Khenen-su lived the Phoenix — the 'Great Bennu'. It resembled an eagle, and had feathers of red and golden colour. Some authorities identify this mythical bird with the planet Venus, which, as the morning star, was 'the guide of the sun god'.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XIV.

title.en: Her-shef the Self-created: Head in Heaven, Feet on Earth
title.zh: 自生之神赫爾-舍夫：首在蒼天，足在大地

region.en: Heracleopolis Magna (temple of Her-shef, its chief god)
region.zh: 埃及赫拉克利奧波利斯（其主神赫爾-舍夫神廟）

texts.period: Heracleopolitan state cult, 9th-10th Dynasties onward; retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XIV, 'Father Gods and Mother Goddesses'

summary.en: The chief god of Heracleopolis is a self-created Great Father: his head in the heavens and his feet upon the earth, his right eye the sun and his left the moon, his soul the light he sheds over the world — and he breathes from his nostrils the north wind that gives life to every living being, for 'wind' and 'breath' and 'spirit' were one word to the Egyptians.
summary.zh: 赫拉克利奧波利斯主神乃自生之偉大父神：首在蒼天、足在大地；右眼為日、左眼為月；其魂即其照世之光——且自鼻息中呼出賦生於萬物之北風，蓋『風』『息』『靈』於埃及人本為一詞。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: The chief god was Her-shef, who bears a stronger resemblance to Ptah Tanen than to Horus. He was a self-created Great Father, whose head was in the heavens while his feet rested upon the earth. His right eye was the sun and his left the moon, while his soul was the light that he shed over the world. He breathed from his nostrils the north wind, which gave life to every living being.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XIV.

passages.text: 'Wind' and 'breath' and 'spirit' were believed by many primitive peoples to be identical. Her-shef was therefore the source of universal life. As a 'wind god' he resembles the southern deity Khnumu, who was also called Knef (the Kneph of the Greeks). The Egyptian knef means 'wind', 'breath', and 'spirit' — 'the air of life'.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XIV.

title.en: The Arch of Nut: From Eastern Toes to Western Fingertips
title.zh: 努特之拱：自東足至西指尖

region.en: The sky over Egypt (the body-arch of the sky-goddess)
region.zh: 埃及上空（天神身軀之拱）

texts.period: The Heliopolitan creation cosmology, retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. I, 'Creation Legend of Sun Worshippers'

summary.en: The picture every Egyptian knew: Ra commands earth and heaven to rise from the waste of water, and Shu the uplifter raises Nut on high — she forms the vault arched over Seb, who lies prostrate beneath her, from where at the eastern horizon she is poised upon her toes to where at the western horizon, bending with outstretched arms, she rests upon her finger tips; in the darkness the stars sparkle upon her unwearied limbs.
summary.zh: 每個埃及人都熟悉的圖景：拉命大地與蒼天自洪荒之水升起，『舉天者』舒將努特高舉——她成拱頂，覆於俯臥之塞布其上，自東方地平以足尖點立，至西方地平則屈身舒臂，以指尖著地；黑暗中，星宿閃耀於她不知疲倦的肢體之上。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cosmology retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: Then came into being Seb, the earth god, and Nut, the goddess of the firmament, who became the parents of Osiris and his consort Isis and also of Set and his consort Nepthys. Ra spake at the beginning of Creation, and bade the earth and the heavens to rise out of the waste of water. In the brightness of his majesty they appeared, and Shu, the uplifter, raised Nut upon high. She formed the vault, which is arched over Seb, the god of earth, who lies prostrate beneath her from where, at the eastern horizon, she is poised upon her toes to where, at the western horizon, bending down with outstretched arms, she rests upon her finger tips. In the darkness are beheld the stars which sparkle upon her body and over her great unwearied limbs.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. I.

passages.text: When Ra, according to his desire, uttered the deep thoughts of his mind, that which he named had being. When he gazed into space, that which he desired to see appeared before him. He created all things that move in the waters and upon the dry land. Now, mankind were born from his eye, and Ra, the Creator, who was ruler of the gods, became the first king upon earth. He went about among men; he took form like unto theirs, and to him the centuries were as years.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. I.

title.en: Sebek the Crocodile: The Radiant Green Disk of the Fayum
title.zh: 鱷神塞貝克：法尤姆的翠綠日盤

region.en: Crocodilopolis, the Fayum, Egypt (the sacred lake of the tamed crocodile)
region.zh: 埃及法尤姆鱷城（馴鱷聖湖）

texts.period: Cult of the 12th-13th Dynasties onward (observed by Herodotus and Strabo); retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XVIII, 'Myths and Lays of the Middle Kingdom'

summary.en: The crocodile god of the Middle Kingdom rose to prominence with the Fayum kings: Sebek is 'the radiant green disk — the creator', who rose from Nu 'in many shapes and in many colours'; at Ombos he is the earth giant 'husband of his mother'; and in the sacred lake of Crocodilopolis lived his living image — a tame crocodile with crystal-set golden earrings and bracelets on its fore paws, fed by its priests with cakes, flesh and honey wine.
summary.zh: 中王國鱷神隨法尤姆諸王而興：塞貝克乃『放射之翠綠日盤——創造者』，自努『以多形多色』升起；在翁博斯為『母之夫』的大地巨人；而在鱷城聖湖中則有其活像——馴鱷戴金耳環嵌水晶、前爪有鐲，祭司以餅、肉與蜜酒飼之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: Along with the new royal faces new religious beliefs also came into prominence. The rise of Sebek, the crocodile god, may have been due to the tendency shown by certain of the Pharaohs to reside in the Fayum. The town of Crocodilopolis was the chief centre of the hitherto obscure Sebek cult. — Sebek-Tum-Ra ultimately became the crocodile of the sun, as Mentu became 'bull of the sun', and he symbolized the power and heat of the orb of day. In this form he was the 'radiant green disk' — 'the creator', who rose from Nu 'in many shapes and in many colours'.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XVIII.

passages.text: At Ombos, Sebek was a form of Seb, the earth giant, the son of Nut, and 'husband of his mother'. He was called the 'father of the gods' and 'chief of the Nine Bow Barbarians'. — But his worshippers believed that he would lead souls by 'short cuts' and byways to the Egyptian paradise. In the Pyramid Texts he has the attributes of the elfin Khnumu... for he renews the eyes of the dead, touches their tongues so that they can speak, and restores the power of motion to their heads.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XVIII.

passages.text: Strabo, who visited Egypt in the Roman period, relates that he saw a sacred crocodile in an artificial lake at Crocodilopolis in the Fayum. It was quite tame and was decorated with gold ear-rings, set with crystal, and wore bracelets on its fore paws. The priests opened its jaws and fed it with cakes, flesh, and honey wine. When the animal leapt into the water and came up at the other side, the priests followed it and gave it a fresh offering.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XVIII, citing Strabo.

title.en: Neith the Veiled: The Unknown One Whose Veil Was Never Raised
title.zh: 蒙面之奈特：面紗未曾掀起之未知者

region.en: Sais, Western Delta, Egypt (temple of Neith, the Libyan Great Mother)
region.zh: 埃及西三角洲薩伊斯（利比亞大母神奈特神廟）

texts.period: Cult of Neith from predynastic Libya through the 26th Dynasty (recorded in Mackenzie 1913 and Plutarch)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XVIII, 'Myths and Lays of the Middle Kingdom'

summary.en: In the Pyramid Texts Sebek is the son of Neith, the Libyan Earth Mother, who personified the female principle and was self-sustaining as she had been self-produced: 'the unknown one' and 'the hidden one', whose veil had never been uplifted — like other virgin goddesses she had a fatherless son, 'the husband of his mother'.
summary.zh: 金字塔文中塞貝克乃奈特之子——利比亞大地母神，體現女性本原，自足如自生：『未知者』『隱者』，其面紗未曾掀起——如他處女神，育無父之子，即『母之夫』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling. Cross-refers to the Sais veil inscription cut from Plutarch.

passages.text: In the texts of Unas, Sebek is referred to as the son of Neith, the Libyan 'Earth Mother', who personified the female principle, and was believed to be self-sustaining, as she had been self-produced. She was 'the unknown one' and 'the hidden one', whose veil had never been uplifted. Like other virgin goddesses, she had a fatherless son, the 'husband of his mother', who may have been identified with Sebek as a result of early tribal fusion.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XVIII.

passages.text: To this purpose, likewise, is that inscription which they have engraved upon the base of the statue of Athene at Sais, whom they identify with Isis: 'I am everything that has been, that is, and that shall be: and my veil no man hath raised.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch, De Iside sec. IX, quoted here as the Sais-temple parallel to the Neith tradition.

title.en: The Lay of the Harper: Drink, for No One Returns
title.zh: 琴師之歌：飲吧，無人復返

region.en: Egyptian banquet halls (the skeleton carried round at feasts; symbolic pin, Thebes)
region.zh: 埃及宴廳（宴中巡示之骷髏；象徵定位，底比斯）

texts.period: Song of the Old Kingdom type, sung at banquets into the Middle Kingdom (metrical rendering in Mackenzie 1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XVIII, 'The Lay of the Harper'

summary.en: Egypt's great carpe-diem song, chanted at banquets while a model coffin was carried round: 'No soul comes back to tell us how he fares... Where are the tombs of Imhotep and Hordadaf? Long fallen, their places unknown... Revel in pleasure while your life endures and deck your head with myrrh... for no man takes his riches to the grave; yea, none returns again when he goes hence.'
summary.zh: 埃及最著名之及時行樂之歌，宴中偕小棺巡示而詠：『無魂歸來告我以彼界之事……英霍特普與霍爾代代夫之墓安在？傾頹無跡……趁生而行樂，以沒藥飾首……無人能攜富貴入墓；離去者無一復返。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient banquet song in Mackenzie's metrical rendering; passages verbatim from the rendering. The skeleton custom matches the Maneros record cut from Plutarch.

passages.text: One of the most popular Egyptian poems is called 'The Lay of the Harper'. It was chanted at the banquets given by wealthy men. 'Ere the company rises,' wrote Herodotus, 'a small coffin which contains a perfect model of the human body is carried round, and is shown to each guest in rotation. He who bears it exclaims: Look at this figure. After death you will be like it. Drink, therefore, and be merry.' The 'lay' in its earliest form was of great antiquity. Probably a real mummy was originally hauled through the banquet hall.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XVIII introduction.

passages.text: 'Tis well with this good prince; his day is done, His happy fate fulfilled. So one goes forth While others, as in days of old, remain. The old kings slumber in their pyramids, Likewise the noble and the learned, but some Who builded tombs have now no place of rest, Although their deeds were great. Lo! I have heard The words Imhotep and Hordadaf spake — Their maxims men repeat. Where are their tombs? Long fallen, e'en their places are unknown, And they are now as though they ne'er had been.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), the Lay of the Harper, first stanza.

passages.text: No soul comes back to tell us how he fares — To soothe and comfort us ere we depart Whither he went betimes. But let our minds Forget of this and dwell on better things. Revel in pleasure while your life endures And deck your head with myrrh. Be richly clad In white and perfumed linen; like the gods Anointed be; and never weary grow In eager quest of what your heart desires — Do as it prompts you, until that sad day Of lamentation comes, when hearts at rest Hear not the cry of mourners at the tomb, Which have no meaning to the silent dead. Then celebrate this festal time, nor pause — For no man takes his riches to the grave; Yea, none returns again when he goes hence.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), the Lay of the Harper, closing stanza.
